lead: This unit explains how the transport layer moves data between applications. After reading, students can describe UDP and TCP services, set up connections, and analyse flow and congestion control.
about: Unit 5 consists of eight chapters. Chapter 5.1 introduces transport services, ports, and the multiplexing‑demultiplexing mechanism. Chapter 5.2 covers the User Datagram Protocol. Chapter 5.3 details TCP services and the segment format. Chapter 5.4 explains TCP connection establishment and release. Chapter 5.5 (advanced) discusses TCP flow control using sliding windows. Chapter 5.6 examines TCP congestion control, slow start and fast retransmit. Chapter 5.7 presents quality of service and integrated services concepts. Chapter 5.8 introduces the Stream Control Transmission Protocol. Each chapter builds on the previous one, forming a complete picture of transport‑layer operation.

chapters.idea: Transport services use ports to multiplex and demultiplex data for many applications on a host.
chapters.depth: Define port number (16‑bit), socket (IP + port), and how the OS maps incoming datagrams to the correct process. Mention alternative names such as endpoint, service access point, and demultiplexer used in some syllabi.

figure.title: Port multiplexing
figure.aria: Shows two applications on each host using different port numbers and how the transport layer routes packets to the correct application.

chapters.example: Host A runs App 1 on port 5000 and App 2 on port 5001. Host B runs App 3 on port 6000 and App 4 on port 6001. App 1 sends a 120‑byte UDP datagram to App 3. The OS on Host B examines the destination port 6000, matches it to App 3, and delivers the payload.
chapters.trap: Confusing the port number with the IP address of the host.
chapters.leave: Socket‑API programming details are covered in Unit 6.

chapters.idea: UDP provides a simple, connection‑less service with minimal header overhead.
chapters.depth: Explain UDP header fields: source port, destination port, length, checksum. Show how length = header (8 bytes) + data size. Mention that some syllabi call it a datagram service.

figure.title: UDP header
figure.aria: Displays the five fields of a UDP segment and the relationship between data length and total segment length.

chapters.example: A DNS query of 32 bytes is sent from source port 12345 to the DNS server port 53. UDP length = 8 (header) + 32 (data) = 40 bytes. The checksum is computed as 0x1A2B (example value).
chapters.trap: Assuming UDP guarantees delivery or ordering.
chapters.leave: Reliability mechanisms are introduced in the TCP chapters.

chapters.idea: TCP offers a reliable byte‑stream service with a rich segment header.
chapters.depth: List TCP header fields: src/dst ports, sequence number, acknowledgment number, data offset, flags, window, checksum, urgent pointer, options. Explain the purpose of each field. Some syllabi refer to it as a connection‑oriented transport protocol.

figure.title: TCP header
figure.aria: Shows each field of a TCP segment, highlighting the SYN flag used during connection setup.

chapters.example: A client sends a TCP SYN segment to a web server. Source port = 34567, destination port = 80, sequence number = 1000, acknowledgment number = 0, data offset = 5 (no options), flags = SYN, window = 65535, checksum = 0xB1C2.
chapters.trap: Reading the data‑offset field as the total segment length instead of the header length in 32‑bit words.
chapters.leave: Detailed option handling is covered in later chapters.

chapters.idea: TCP establishes and releases connections with a three‑way handshake and a four‑step termination.
chapters.depth: Describe the SYN, SYN‑ACK, ACK exchange for setup and the FIN, ACK, FIN, ACK exchange for teardown. Mention that some syllabi call this connection management or connection lifecycle.

figure.aria: Shows the three‑way handshake followed by the four‑step termination between client and server.

chapters.example: Client A chooses ISN = 2000 and sends SYN. Server B replies with ISN = 3000 and ACK = 2001. Client acknowledges with ACK = 3001. After data exchange, Client sends FIN with seq = 2500, Server ACKs, then Server sends its own FIN with seq = 3001, and Client ACKs, closing the connection.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to increment the sequence number after sending a SYN (the SYN consumes one sequence number).
chapters.leave: Flow‑control details are covered in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: TCP flow control uses a sliding window advertised by the receiver to avoid overflow.
chapters.depth: Explain the receive window field, how the sender limits outstanding bytes, and the concept of zero‑window probing. Only a few universities teach this in depth, so keep the description concise.

figure.title: Sliding window
figure.aria: Illustrates how the sender can transmit only up to the advertised receive window size.

chapters.example: Sender has a congestion window of 5 KB but the receiver advertises a receive window of 3 KB. The sender may transmit only 3 KB of data before waiting for a new ACK that increases the advertised window.
chapters.trap: Mixing the receive window with the congestion window and limiting traffic twice.

chapters.idea: TCP congestion control adjusts the sending rate using slow start and fast retransmit.
chapters.depth: Detail slow start (cwnd doubles each RTT), transition to congestion avoidance (linear increase), detection of loss via triple duplicate ACKs, fast retransmit, and setting ssthresh. Some syllabi also mention fast recovery, which will be omitted here.

figure.aria: Shows exponential growth of cwnd during slow start and the reduction to ssthresh after a loss event.

chapters.example: Initial cwnd = 1 MSS. After RTT 1 → 2 MSS, RTT 2 → 4 MSS, RTT 3 → 8 MSS. A loss is detected by three duplicate ACKs at RTT 4. ssthresh is set to cwnd/2 = 4 MSS, cwnd is reduced to 4 MSS, and slow start ends.
chapters.trap: Assuming slow start continues indefinitely without switching to congestion avoidance.
chapters.leave: Quality‑of‑service concepts are covered in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Quality of Service (QoS) provides differentiated treatment for traffic classes across the network.
chapters.depth: Introduce Integrated Services (IntServ) and Differentiated Services (DiffServ). Explain DSCP values, traffic shaping, and simple bandwidth allocation calculations. Some syllabi list QoS under resource allocation.

figure.aria: Shows where QoS markings (DSCP) reside in the protocol stack.

chapters.example: An ISP offers 4 Mbps for video (DSCP = 46) and 1 Mbps for web (DSCP = 0). On a 10 Mbps link the video flow uses 4 Mbps, web uses 1 Mbps, leaving 5 Mbps for best‑effort traffic.
chapters.trap: Confusing QoS guarantees with reliability mechanisms like retransmission.
chapters.leave: The next chapter introduces the newer transport protocol SCTP.

chapters.idea: SCTP provides a reliable, message‑oriented transport service with multi‑streaming and multi‑homing.
chapters.depth: Describe the four‑step handshake with cookie, the concept of streams, and the association identifier. Some syllabi refer to SCTP as a transport‑layer extension.

figure.aria: Illustrates SCTP’s four‑step handshake using a cookie and the subsequent data exchange on a chosen stream.

chapters.example: Client initiates with ISN = 5000. Server replies with a cookie value 0x9A. Client returns the cookie in COOKIE‑ECHO. Server validates and sends COOKIE‑ACK with association ID = 100. The client then sends a DATA chunk on stream 1 containing the text "Hello".
chapters.trap: Treating SCTP as if it had only a single stream like TCP.
